content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors show that a novel class of flow-based neural networks can approximate local diffeomorphisms between manifolds.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
-----------
* The paper presents interesting analysis about learning local diffeomorphisms between manifolds (including manifolds that have some added amount of noise and varying topologies).

Weaknesses
---------------
* While this paper is highly theoretical and thus applications may be hard to find, it should be noted that the real-world neural networks that are used as motivating examples are rather niche. In particular, the proposed network architecture in the proofs is not yet deployed in practice (as far as I know), which undercuts the paper's viability/appeal.
* There are several weaknesses that I point out in the next section for both clarity, novelty, and technical accuracy. As a highlight: 1) the paper is incredibly difficult to read and needs many edits for this direction, 2) the results feel rather weak and (related to the above) overly technical for the specific domain, and 3) there exist many technical errors in early proofs.
* The additional examples of applications are very underdeveloped. In particular, Theorem 4 is the only interesting example, as the others don't have any technical consequence (they basically are corollaries of the main result). The example on Cryo-Em is especially weak because it is effectively an example of the work done in section 3.1, and 1 out of the 3 paragraphs is just there to point out that orbifolds exist would be something better to consider.
* A massive concern that I have about this paper is that it's effectively a (rather niche + sub-par) differential geometry paper being submitted as a machine learning theory paper. In particular, it should be noted that almost all of the analysis that is done is done without much regard for neural network approximation capability (e.g. neural networks are universal approximators and everything else is waived). Instead, the analysis focuses on developing analytic properties of manifolds and their function classes, which is something that's not really in the scope of a machine learning conference. While this was the case for some previous papers (especially in this flow approximation case), the current paper feels even more disconnected.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
-------
I found the paper to be very very hard to read and parse technically. This is due to the overabundance of notation which, although common for papers of this type, feels excessive and unneeded in this instance. In particular, there are several constructions where notation should be drastically reduced and clarified. In addition, the overall presentation is rather poor, as many technical sections include somewhat ancillary technical observations (e.g. page 5 includes a lot of unnecessary analytic facts that are not used later).

Novelty
---------
I'm unsure about the novelty of the paper, as my overall impression I got after reading it was that several of the technical contributions may already exist in part in the broader mathematical literature. In particular, the theorems about local diffeomorphisms feel rather weak (e.g. they are easily seen to be related to coverings), where the long length is primarily constructed to appease other technical conditions (like traingulations and/or universal approximation).

Technical Comments
------------------------
* Def 1: the authors don't define $\mathrm{locdif^1}$ anywhere in the paper($\mathrm{locdif}$ is defined).
* Def 1: Doesn't $\mathcal{F} \neq \emptyset$ this imply that $\mathcal{M}_1$ is $\mathcal{M}_2$-dimensional? The definition states that $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ are $n$-dimensional.
* Lemma 1 proof first part (lipschitz):  Need to show more steps in general (e.g. triangular splitting should be shown, as well as how each term is bounded by the bistable condition). This is necessary for the distance computation especially since it is not apparent since we working over manifolds. I think there is something wrong also (shouldn't effect the outcome of the proof since it's a constant factor), as even the stated conditions don't make sense since it requires $2/\pi d_{M_1}(x_1, x_2) \le \| x - y\|$, not $\pi/2$ as is currently given.
* Lemma 1 proof second part (inverse lipschitz): Again there are extra terms in the computation (e.g. it is implied in one of the equation blocks that$d_{\mathcal{M}_1} = \|\cdot \|$) that should be corrected. This doesn't change the overall proof (as Lipschitzness is still achieved).
* Corr 1: you don't ever use $W^{1, 2}$, so why include it? This is unncessary.
* Example 1: Appendix B.2 is referenced here, but Appendix B.2 only covers the proof of Lemma 1, not the construction of the locally homeomorphic map. Additionally, the information given in Figure 1 seems unrelated and irrelevant.

Theorems 2 and 3
---------------------
It is very hard to parse the proofs of Theorems 2 and 3, but the results align with my expectations. It is very likely, however, that some issues like those that arose in the earlier proofs exist that I may have missed. There are also other general concerns that override this:
* Theorem 2 statement: since proper local diffeomorphisms are already covering maps for connected manifolds (this is an exercise in [1]), it seems to me that the overall statement is just showing that the covering map can be decomposed more directly. Is the interesting thing here the fact that we have an embedding in the middle? Given the extensive differential geometry, I find it hard to believe that something was not previously shown.
* Theorem 2 statement: why are we working with triangulations? This feels somewhat unnecessary (as the results should be triangulation agnostic), adds a lot of overhead to the proofs and the statements, and, if introduced, should be presented separately as a consequence of triangulation.
* Similar comments hold for Theorem 3.


Nitpicks/Typos
-----------------
There are many typos that need to be fixed (they obstruct key statements and proof details). Here is a sparse sampling.
* 2nd page: "many tools in TDA tools" should be changed to avoid double usage
* Sec 1.1: should mathematically introduce what a "fixed projector" is when introducing "p"
* Sec 1.3: "of the form 1" should be replaced to be clear e.g. "of the form given in equation (1)" for clarity
* Notation: I see stuff like $\mathrm{functionclass}^1$ appear a lot and I assume it is differentiable, but this is not included in the appendix introduction so I'm not sure.
* Typo in sec B.2 proof of Lemma 1: $x_2$ instead of $x_x$ in first line of equation, $d_{\mathcal{M]_1}$ instead of $d_X$ in the second equation.
* Theorem 2 statement: the $n$ that appears in $\mathbb{R}^{2n + 1}$ is never defined.

[1] "Manifolds and Differential Geometry" Jeffrey M Lee
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I vote to strongly reject the paper due to the multitude of issues I described above.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this article, the authors study the universal approximation properties of deep neural nets for approximating local diffeomorphisms between smooth submanifolds. They provide template architectures (called extension-projection) that satisfy such properties, and mention a few machine learning problems that can benefit from such results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:

Weaknesses:
---I do not think that this article is accessible and/or understandable for most of the ICLR community. The exposition is way too mathematically heavy and the absence of any numerical experiments make me question the suitability of this work to the ICLR conference.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces the theoretical underpinnings of an architecture that combines invertible flows, and a fixed projection layer, with injective expansions layers is a universal approximator of maps between manifolds. This architecture, realized in extension projection networks of a particular form,  is capable of learning maps with locally stable inverses between topologically complex manifolds. Crucially, the architecture does not assume any prior knowledge of the topology of the starting and target manifolds.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I think the theoretical results which use bistable local approximations forming a homeomorphism is interesting and would provide a guide to the design of such a network. 

However, I think the writing of this work is inaccessible to most ICLR readers. By contrast if you look at the work in Puthwala 2022, this is written from a basis in existing neural network frameworks where the contribution is clear. 

First, the TDA sections are not really necessary. There is not much work in deep learning that tries to use TDA in any fashion to map from manifolds to manifolds,  Rather TDA is used to featurize or characterize manifolds. Works that use pseudo-invertible embeddings of manifolds sometimes use topological quantities to preserve certain information but is not used as the basis for the mapping [Moor 2019]. Rather than use space for this the authors should make the form of their proposal very clear using a schematic of their proposed network architectural framework with numerous examples. 

Although universal approximators don't have to be used for training [for example cybenko's 1989 sigmoidal superpositions], in this work it would be useful to highlight a practical example. The  main  contribution  of  this  work  is  to  establish  that  extension-projection  networks  can  universally approximate mappings that are diffeomorphisms locally but change topology globally.  Practically this can be applied to generative problems, where the architecture allows for flexibility  in the choice of the starting manifold, where one can sample from a base distribution to generate  data  via  a  learned  mapping  to  a  more  complex  target  manifold.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The  material  presented  in  the appendix  is  not  optional  reading,  for  experts  and  non-experts  alike,  to  fully  understand  this 
paper so material on TDA and group invariant networks could be switched out to the appendix in favor of material in appendix A.
content.summary_of_the_review: The manuscript contains universality results for extension-projection network mapping between manifolds, but the writing, and utility of the results is unclear the way it is written.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper deals with maps between smooth compact C-infinity manifolds that are locally diffeomorphisms. The paper principal claim is  a proof that any such map can be approximated by a composition of the form TpE, where T is a homeomorphism between affine spaces, p is a map which can be taken as a coordinate projection, and E is again some composition, which consists of arbitrary homeomorphisms and injective continuos maps.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: the paper mentions topology in a discussion aimed at approximation properties of the neural networks, topology can be relevant in various machine learning contexts especially in what concerns existences of global topological obstructions.

Weaknesses: clarity, quality, novelty and reproducibility are problematic, see below
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity of the work is poor. Numerous sentences are incomplete, imprecise or seemingly erroneous. This includes statements of the central theorems. E.g. « Theorem 1. Let n0 =n,nL =m,M⊂Rn be a compact k-manifold for n≥3k+1,μ∈calP(M1),and be an absolutely continuous.» 
A reader struggles to understand here which mathematical object is concerned by the property « be an absolutely continuous ».  Also the notation calP(M1) is not explained anywhere in the paper, including the appendix.

Quality and novelty are not sufficient. The paper starts from several erroneous claims, such as: 
« Other approaches not utilizing TDA exist and are able to learn mappings between submanifolds, but only when the manifolds to be learned have simple topology. That is, they only apply to manifolds that are given by a single chart and so can’t learn mappings that change topology » - it is commonly known that architectures with ReLu activations do not produce homeomorphisms and thus they CAN learn mappings that change topology.  

The relevance of the paper’s main problematics of approximating C-infinty smooth local diffeomorphisms between  C-infinity smooth manifolds to the machine learning community is not supported by any arguments. The « data manifolds » encountered in the machine learning context as supports of data distributions are rarely smooth C-infinity manifolds  and maps between them are quite often non-differentiable. 
 
Even mathematical novelty of the result is not quite clear as the claims are not well placed in connection with the literature on the subject. There is an extensive math literature on decompositions into injections-projections for C-infinity smooth maps, e.g.  (Topology Appl. 140 (2004), 133–149).  

Reproducibility is questionable as any details concerning the experimental part on cryo-EM are absent.
content.summary_of_the_review:
- Clarity of the work is poor.
- Quality and novelty are not sufficient.
- Reproducibility is questionable.
- A connection of the papers' topic to data analysis tasks is not very clear. 
The style of the paper is such that it looks like ICLR is not an appropriate venue for the paper. I do not think that the paper is of significant interest for ICLR community.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewers for taking the time to review the manuscript and in particular reviewers Du9G and et5J for their specific and detailed feedback.
 
We have decided to withdraw the manuscript from consideration at ICLR 2023. We stand by both the novelty and significance of our work both mathematically and in its application to machine learning. It is, to our knowledge, the first work of its kind to draw connections between the topology of abstract covering spaces on manifolds as a model space and the desire to learn locally stable mappings in manifold learning. We also believe that our proposed network is the first to identify these abstract projections with a simple coordinate projection, thus enabling us to universally learn topologically non-trivial mappings.
 
That said, it is very difficult to include all your good suggestions for the work within the two-week revision window, as they require some time to implement correctly. Your feedback has painted a clear picture of how the introduction can be restructured to make the transition into the topological details clearer. Further, we have gained insight into notations and language that may be confusing to future readers.
 
Thank you again for your reviews and suggestions.
